newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS - City of Prague defies cbank, govt with bond.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - City of Prague defies cbank, govt with bond.

text.p: The City of Prague assembly, against government and central bank wishes, approved a plan on Friday to issue up to nine billion crowns ($278.9 million) through an international bond issue.

Government and central bank officials have warned the city against going ahead with the issue because it would bring a large amount of new funds into circulation at a time when authorities are struggling to keep the money supply in check.
But the assembly approved the plan, anyway, adding the condition that the issue would have a maturity of either five, seven or 10 years, depending on market conditions.
The assembly must still decide the currency in which it will issue the bonds, and city officials have said they would like to launch the paper sometime before the end of the year.
Six billion crowns of the money raised will be used for infrastructure projects, while the remainder will be kept in a housing fund.

"Three billion crowns of this will be money that should not enter circulation," said Prague Mayor Jan Koukal in response to official concerns over where the money will end up and what its effect on the economy will be.
Both the government and central bank have criticised the idea of Prague issuing a bond, given the government's current battle to restrict demand and keep spending in line.
Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said the issue would be acceptable only if the city did not dissolve the capital.
Koukal said funds from the issue would not be thrown "all at once" into the economy, and that the Finance Ministry had given a preliminary positive stance on the issue.
But a senior ministry official, who asked not to be named, said that the ministry could set unattainable conditions for issuance of the bonds if it wants to stop it.
The Finance Ministry has final approval of any bond issue by a municipality.
Ministry spokeswoman Ludmila Nutilova would not say how the ministry would react to the approval of the plan. Central bank officials were not immediately available for comment.

The Czech economy was shaken in late May by a speculative attack on the crown which forced the central bank to float the currency and it fell to more than 15 percent below its highs against the dollar and mark in early February.

The controlled float of the currency was backed by a rise in key interest rates and a government austerity package meant to slow domestic demand and dampen the inflationary effects of the crown's depreciation.
Prague carries an indicative investment-grade "A" rating from Standard & Poor's, the same as the Czech sovereign debt.
It last entered foreign markets in 1994 with a $250 million five-year Eurobond.
